questions.stem: Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed using graphite electrodes. What forms at each electrode?
options: Bromine at the cathode and lead at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and bromine at the anode
Lead at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Lead at the cathode and bromine at the anode
questions.explanation: A molten salt contains only its own ions, so Pb²⁺ is reduced to lead at the negative cathode and Br⁻ is oxidised to bromine at the positive anode. Hydrogen and oxygen come from water, and there is no water in a molten salt.

questions.stem: Why is the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻, not oxidised at the anode when sodium sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes?
options: Sulfur is already in its maximum oxidation state of +6
Sulfate ions are attracted to the cathode, not the anode
Sulfate ions are too large to reach the electrode surface
Sulfur is in its lowest oxidation state of −2 in sulfate
questions.explanation: Oxidation is an increase in oxidation number, and sulfur in SO₄²⁻ is already at +6, the highest it can reach. Water is oxidised at the anode instead. Being negative, sulfate ions do move towards the anode; they simply cannot lose electrons there.

questions.stem: Sodium sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. E°: Na⁺/Na −2.71 V, 2H₂O/H₂ −0.83 V, O₂/H₂O +1.23 V. What forms at each electrode?
options: Sodium at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and sulfur dioxide at the anode
Sodium at the cathode and sulfur at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
questions.explanation: Water is a stronger oxidising agent than Na⁺, so water is reduced to hydrogen at the cathode. Sulfate cannot be oxidised further, so water is oxidised to oxygen at the anode. The sodium sulfate only makes the solution conduct.

questions.stem: In the electrolysis of sodium sulfate solution with inert electrodes, 40 mL of hydrogen is collected at the cathode. Assuming both gases are at the same temperature and pressure, what volume of oxygen forms at the anode?
options: 80 mL
10 mL
20 mL
40 mL
questions.explanation: The half-equations are 4H₂O + 4e⁻ → 2H₂ + 4OH⁻ and 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻. The same 4 mol of electrons gives 2 mol of H₂ but only 1 mol of O₂, so the oxygen volume is half the hydrogen volume.

questions.stem: Sodium chloride solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. E° values predict oxygen at the anode (O₂/H₂O +1.23 V, Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36 V), yet a concentrated solution gives mainly chlorine. Why is the prediction wrong?
options: E° values apply only to molten salts, never to aqueous solutions of the salts
Chloride ions are stronger oxidising agents than water at every concentration
Oxygen is produced first but reacts with the sodium ions to form chlorine gas
E° values apply to standard conditions, and here the chloride concentration is high
questions.explanation: The electrochemical series is based on 1 mol/L solutions at 25 °C. When the chloride concentration is far from standard and the two E° values are close, chloride can be oxidised in preference to water. This is a limitation of predicting electrolysis products from E° values alone.

questions.stem: Which statement about predicting electrolysis products from the electrochemical series is correct?
options: The strongest oxidising agent present is usually reduced at the cathode
The strongest reducing agent present is usually reduced at the cathode
The strongest oxidising agent present is usually oxidised at the anode
The weakest reducing agent present is usually oxidised at the anode
questions.explanation: At the cathode, electrons are gained by the species that accepts them most readily, the strongest oxidising agent. At the anode, the strongest reducing agent present gives up electrons. Concentration and electrode material can change this, which is why the word usually matters.

questions.stem: A brass key is to be electroplated with nickel. Which set-up is correct?
options: Key as the anode, nickel cathode, nickel(II) sulfate electrolyte
Key as the cathode, graphite anode, sodium sulfate electrolyte
Key as the anode, graphite cathode, nickel(II) sulfate electrolyte
Key as the cathode, nickel anode, nickel(II) sulfate electrolyte
questions.explanation: Ni²⁺ ions are reduced to nickel at the cathode, so the key must be the cathode in a solution of Ni²⁺. A nickel anode is oxidised to Ni²⁺, replacing the ions used. Sodium sulfate contains no nickel, so nothing could plate from it.

questions.stem: During nickel electroplating with a nickel anode, why does the concentration of Ni²⁺ in the electrolyte stay roughly constant?
options: The Ni²⁺ ions are not reduced, so none are removed from the solution
Water is reduced at the cathode instead of nickel, so the ions remain
The sulfate ions are reduced to replace the nickel ions that are used
Nickel dissolves from the anode as fast as it plates onto the cathode
questions.explanation: At the anode Ni → Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ and at the cathode Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ni. The same charge passes through both electrodes, so ions enter the solution at the rate they leave it. Nickel ions are reduced, which is how the key is plated.

questions.stem: In the electrorefining of copper, where is the impure copper placed?
options: As the anode, where its copper is oxidised to Cu²⁺
As the cathode, where its copper is reduced to Cu²⁺
As the cathode, where pure copper is deposited on it
In the electrolyte, dissolved as copper(II) sulfate
questions.explanation: The impure copper is the anode, so its copper atoms are oxidised and pass into solution. Cu²⁺ ions are then reduced to pure copper on the cathode, a thin sheet of pure copper or a steel blank.

questions.stem: Faraday's first law of electrolysis states that the mass of a substance produced at an electrode is:
options: inversely proportional to the quantity of charge passed
directly proportional to the voltage of the power supply
independent of the time for which the current flows
directly proportional to the quantity of charge passed
questions.explanation: The amount of product depends on the number of electrons transferred, Q = It, so doubling the current or the time doubles the mass. The supply voltage decides whether electrolysis can happen, not how much product forms.

questions.stem: Aluminium is produced by electrolysing molten aluminium oxide. What mass of aluminium is produced by a current of 5.00 A flowing for 2.00 hours? F = 96 485 C/mol, M(Al) = 26.98 g/mol.
questions.explanation: Q = It = 5.00 × 7200 = 36 000 C, so n(e⁻) = 36 000/96 485 = 0.373 mol. Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al, so n(Al) = 0.373/3 = 0.124 mol and the mass is 0.124 × 26.98 = 3.36 g. Forgetting to divide by 3 gives 10.1 g.

questions.stem: What current is needed to deposit 2.00 g of nickel from Ni²⁺(aq) in 45.0 minutes? F = 96 485 C/mol, M(Ni) = 58.69 g/mol.
questions.explanation: n(Ni) = 2.00/58.69 = 0.0341 mol, and two electrons per Ni²⁺ give n(e⁻) = 0.0682 mol. Q = 0.0682 × 96 485 = 6576 C, and I = Q/t = 6576/2700 = 2.44 A. Using 45.0 instead of 2700 s gives the very large value.

questions.stem: A current of 0.600 A passed for 1.50 hours deposits 0.582 g of chromium (M = 52.00 g/mol) from a solution of a chromium salt. F = 96 485 C/mol. What is the charge on the chromium ions?
questions.explanation: Q = 0.600 × 5400 = 3240 C, so n(e⁻) = 3240/96 485 = 0.0336 mol. n(Cr) = 0.582/52.00 = 0.0112 mol. The ratio of electrons to chromium atoms is 3, so the ions are Cr³⁺.

questions.stem: Cells containing silver nitrate solution and molten aluminium oxide are connected in series, and 2.16 g of silver is deposited. What mass of aluminium forms in the same time? M(Ag) = 107.87, M(Al) = 26.98 g/mol.
questions.explanation: In series the same charge passes through both cells. n(Ag) = 2.16/107.87 = 0.0200 mol = n(e⁻), and each Al³⁺ needs 3 electrons, so n(Al) = 0.00668 mol and the mass is 0.180 g. Multiplying by 3 instead of dividing gives 1.62 g.

questions.stem: How long must a current of 4.00 A flow to plate 3.00 g of zinc from Zn²⁺(aq) onto a steel object? F = 96 485 C/mol, M(Zn) = 65.38 g/mol.
options: 2.21 minutes
36.9 minutes
18.4 minutes
73.8 minutes
questions.explanation: n(Zn) = 3.00/65.38 = 0.0459 mol, so n(e⁻) = 0.0918 mol and Q = 0.0918 × 96 485 = 8855 C. t = Q/I = 8855/4.00 = 2214 s, which is 36.9 minutes. Leaving out the factor of 2 for Zn²⁺ halves the time.

questions.stem: In chemistry, corrosion of a metal is best described as:
options: oxidation of the metal by substances in its environment
reduction of the metal by oxygen and water in the air
the metal melting slowly because of heat from the Sun
the metal dissolving in water without any electron transfer
questions.explanation: Corrosion is a redox process in which the metal loses electrons, usually to oxygen with water present. Metal atoms become ions, so the metal is oxidised, not reduced.

questions.stem: Iron nails are left for a week in three sealed tubes: dry air, boiled water under a layer of oil, and ordinary tap water open to air. Which nail rusts?
options: Only the nail in tap water open to air
Only the nail in boiled water under oil
Only the nail in the dry air
All three nails rust to the same extent
questions.explanation: Rusting needs both water and oxygen. Dry air has no water, and boiling removes dissolved oxygen while the oil stops it dissolving again. Only the nail in tap water open to air has both.

questions.stem: When iron rusts in a drop of water, which half-equation occurs at the cathode?
options: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻
Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻
Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Fe
4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻
questions.explanation: Dissolved oxygen is reduced at the cathode, gaining the electrons released by iron at the anode. Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ is the anode reaction. The OH⁻ formed then meets Fe²⁺ to start forming rust.

questions.stem: Rust is mostly hydrated iron(III) oxide. Which formula represents it?
options: Fe₃O₄·xH₂O
Fe₂O₃·xH₂O
FeO·xH₂O
Fe(OH)₂
questions.explanation: Fe²⁺ and OH⁻ form Fe(OH)₂, which oxygen oxidises further to iron(III) compounds that lose water to give Fe₂O₃·xH₂O. The x shows that the amount of water varies. Fe(OH)₂ is an early product, not rust itself.

questions.stem: A drop of salt water containing ferroxyl indicator is placed on clean steel. Blue colour appears at the centre of the drop and pink near its edge. What does this show?
options: Fe²⁺ forms at the centre, the cathode; OH⁻ forms at the edge, the anode
Fe³⁺ forms at the edge, the anode; H⁺ forms at the centre, the cathode
Fe²⁺ forms at the centre, the anode; OH⁻ forms at the edge, the cathode
OH⁻ forms at the centre, the anode; Fe²⁺ forms at the edge, the cathode
questions.explanation: Ferroxyl indicator turns blue with Fe²⁺ and pink, through its phenolphthalein, with OH⁻. Iron is oxidised under the centre of the drop, the anode, while oxygen is reduced to OH⁻ near the edge, the cathode.

questions.stem: Why does the cathode in a corroding water drop form near the edge of the drop rather than at its centre?
options: Salt collects at the edge, and salt is reduced in place of dissolved oxygen
The water is deepest at the edge, so more water molecules can be reduced
Oxygen dissolves from the air, so its concentration is highest near the edge
Iron is more reactive near the edge, so electrons are released there first
questions.explanation: The cathode reaction needs oxygen, which is replenished fastest where the drop is thinnest, at its edge. Under the centre, oxygen is scarce, so that region becomes the anode where iron is oxidised. Salt ions carry charge but are not themselves reduced.

questions.stem: Two regions of the same steel plate are in contact with water. Region P has much more dissolved oxygen than region Q. What happens?
options: An electrochemical cell forms, with Q as the anode where iron corrodes
An electrochemical cell forms, with P as the anode where iron corrodes
No cell can form because both regions are made of the same metal
Both regions corrode at the same rate because the metal is the same
questions.explanation: A difference in oxygen concentration is enough to set up a cell, even on one piece of metal. Oxygen is reduced where it is plentiful, at P, which becomes the cathode. The oxygen-poor region Q becomes the anode, which is why steel corrodes under deposits and in crevices.

questions.stem: An iron nail bent in the middle is left in salt water. Where does rusting begin first?
options: Evenly over the whole nail, because it is all the same metal
Only at the head, because it is furthest from the bend
At the bend, because stressed metal forms anodes more readily
Along the straight sections, because they are less stressed
questions.explanation: Metal atoms in stressed regions, such as the bend, the head and the point of a nail, are more easily oxidised, so these regions tend to become anodes. The unstressed parts act as cathodes, where oxygen is reduced.

questions.stem: Cars in coastal towns, or on roads salted in winter, rust faster than cars kept in dry inland areas. Why do dissolved salts speed up corrosion?
options: The ions react directly with iron atoms, replacing oxygen in the corrosion reaction
The ions raise the electrode potential of iron so that it becomes a stronger oxidant
The ions lower the amount of oxygen in the water so that iron is oxidised by salt
The ions make the water a better electrolyte, carrying charge between anode and cathode
questions.explanation: Corrosion is a cell whose internal circuit is the water film. Dissolved ions increase its conductivity, so charge moves between anodic and cathodic sites more easily and the iron corrodes faster. Oxygen is still the species reduced.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts the bonding in steel and in rust?
options: Steel has ionic bonding, while rust has metallic bonding
Both have metallic bonding, but rust contains water
Steel has covalent bonding, while rust has ionic bonding
Steel has metallic bonding, while rust has ionic bonding
questions.explanation: Steel is mostly iron atoms held in a lattice by delocalised electrons. Rust is an ionic compound of Fe³⁺, O²⁻ and water. The change in bonding explains why their properties are so different.

questions.stem: Which property shows that rust no longer has the bonding of the steel it came from?
options: It is ductile and can be drawn out into thin wires
It is shiny and reflects light when freshly exposed
It is brittle and flaky, and does not conduct electricity
It is malleable and conducts electricity when it is solid
questions.explanation: Rust is an ionic solid, so it is brittle and its ions are fixed, making it a non-conductor. Malleability, ductility, lustre and conduction in the solid all come from metallic bonding, which is what steel has.

questions.stem: Rust occupies a much larger volume than the iron it forms from. Which statement explains this and gives a consequence?
options: Rust has metallic bonding with spaces between atoms, so it bends steel reinforcing rods
Rust absorbs nitrogen from the air as it forms, so it swells and makes paint dissolve
Rust includes oxygen and water and is less dense, so it can crack concrete around steel
Rust is denser than iron, so it pulls away from the surface and leaves gaps in concrete
questions.explanation: Each iron atom ends up surrounded by oxide ions and water molecules in a less dense, porous solid, so the rust takes up several times the volume of the iron. Rusting reinforcing steel therefore pushes outward and cracks the surrounding concrete. Rust is less dense than iron, not more.

questions.stem: Why does rust give iron little protection once it forms?
options: It reacts with the iron below it, converting the remaining metal to rust
It is porous and flakes off, so water and oxygen keep reaching fresh iron
It is a good conductor, so it carries electrons away from the iron below
It dissolves completely in rain water, washing away as soon as it forms
questions.explanation: The rust layer is brittle, porous and larger in volume than the iron, so it cracks and falls away. Fresh metal is then exposed to water and oxygen and corrosion continues. Rust is a poor conductor, and it does not dissolve readily.

questions.stem: A steel bolt holds a copper sheet on a boat, in contact with sea water. E°: Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V. What happens?
options: Neither metal corrodes because they protect each other
The steel bolt becomes the anode and corrodes faster
The copper sheet becomes the anode and corrodes faster
The steel bolt becomes the cathode and is protected
questions.explanation: Iron is the stronger reducing agent, with the lower E°, so it is oxidised and becomes the anode. Copper becomes the cathode, where oxygen is reduced. The bolt corrodes faster than it would alone.

questions.stem: Galvanised iron is steel coated with a layer of:
options: chromium
zinc
tin
copper
questions.explanation: Galvanising coats steel with zinc, usually by dipping it in molten zinc. Tin plating is used for food cans, and chromium plating mainly for decoration.

questions.stem: Galvanised steel and tin-plated steel are each deeply scratched, exposing the steel. E°: Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V, Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44 V, Sn²⁺/Sn −0.14 V. What happens?
options: In both the coating corrodes instead of the iron, so both stay protected
In both the iron corrodes faster, because each coating becomes a cathode
In galvanised steel zinc corrodes instead of iron; in tin plate the iron corrodes
In galvanised steel the iron corrodes; in tin plate the tin corrodes instead of iron
questions.explanation: Zinc is a stronger reducing agent than iron, so it becomes the anode and is sacrificed while the iron is the cathode. Tin is a weaker reducing agent, so when tin plate is scratched the iron becomes the anode and corrodes faster than bare steel would. Tin is a noble coating that only works while it is unbroken.

questions.stem: Blocks of zinc are bolted to the steel hull of a ship below the waterline. How do they protect the hull?
options: Zinc is oxidised in place of iron, so the hull becomes the cathode
Zinc is reduced in place of iron, so the hull becomes the anode
Zinc forms a coating that seals the whole hull from sea water
Zinc removes the dissolved salt from the water around the hull
questions.explanation: Zinc is the stronger reducing agent, so it is the anode and corrodes, supplying electrons to the hull. The steel becomes the cathode, where oxygen is reduced, so the iron is not oxidised. The blocks are used up and must be replaced.

questions.stem: Which metal could be used as a sacrificial anode to protect a steel water pipe? E°: Mg²⁺/Mg −2.37 V, Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44 V, Pb²⁺/Pb −0.13 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V.
options: Iron
Magnesium
Lead
Copper
questions.explanation: A sacrificial anode must be a stronger reducing agent than iron, with a lower E°, so that it is oxidised first. Magnesium meets this. Lead and copper are weaker reducing agents, so connecting them would make the steel the anode and speed up its corrosion.

questions.stem: A buried steel pipeline is connected to the negative terminal of a DC power supply, with the positive terminal joined to an inert electrode in the soil. What does this achieve?
options: Electrons are forced onto the pipe, making it the cathode so it is not oxidised
Electrons are drawn out of the pipe, making it the anode so rust cannot form
The current heats the pipe, keeping it dry so that water cannot reach the steel
The current reduces the soil, so that no oxygen is left to react with the steel
questions.explanation: This is cathodic protection by an applied EMF. The supply pushes electrons into the pipe, so reduction occurs at its surface rather than oxidation of iron. Making the pipe an anode would speed up its corrosion.

questions.stem: Which method is most suitable for protecting the moving links of a steel bicycle chain from rusting?
options: Coating the chain with a layer of tin
Oiling or greasing the chain regularly
Painting the chain with a thick enamel
Bolting a zinc block onto the frame
questions.explanation: Oil or grease keeps water and oxygen away from the metal and still lets the links move; it can be renewed as it wears off. Paint would crack and flake at the moving joints, and a zinc block on the frame would not form a circuit with the chain through an electrolyte.

questions.stem: How do paint and polymer coatings protect steel from corrosion?
options: They are oxidised in place of iron, acting as sacrificial anodes
They supply electrons to the iron, making it act as a cathode
They react with rust and convert it back into iron metal
They form a barrier that keeps water and oxygen off the metal
questions.explanation: Paint and polymer coatings exclude the environment, so the conditions for rusting are never met. They give no electrochemical protection, so once they are scratched the exposed steel can rust.
